extracted.intended_audience: IPR counsel, patent litigators, petitioners and patent owners participating in PTAB inter partes review proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on obtaining, submitting, and challenging evidence in PTAB inter partes review (IPR) proceedings, including use of corroborating evidence, supplemental information rules, Garmin discovery factors, and motions to exclude or strike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of corroborating evidence to support expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB gives little or no weight to expert testimony that does not disclose the underlying facts or data on which the opinion is based (37 C.F.R. § 42.65). The expert should therefore use corroborating evidence, including patents, papers, and other teachings, to support their testimony and ensure that the PTAB gives it the weight it deserves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an expert’s declaration, IPR counsel should work with the expert to ensure that statements in the declaration are supported or corroborated by the corroborating evidence. Parties should cite corroborating evidence in the expert’s declaration as well as in the paper that references the expert’s testimony to avoid improper incorporation by reference. Corroborating evidence can strengthen assertions about POSITA understanding, motivation to combine, and predictable results, and can help avoid the appearance of impermissible hindsight bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate assertions about a POSITA’s knowledge or understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: When a petitioner or patent owner argues that a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) would have known or understood a particular fact or reached a specific conclusion, cite corroborating evidence (such as additional prior art references) that supports the expert’s assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use corroborating art or teachings to validate assertions about what a POSITA would or would not have known, and to support motivation to combine or predictable results. Petitioners often overlook citing corroborating evidence for a proposed combination; doing so can amplify and validate hypothetical combinations while avoiding hindsight bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uncorroborated or 'copy/paste' expert declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert declarations that merely recite petition language or recapitulate conclusions without explaining the expert’s reasoning or citing supporting evidence will be given little or no weight (see Xerox Corp. v. Bytemark, Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft declarations as vehicles to discuss the expert’s reasoning, include prior art references or other underlying facts/data, and avoid verbatim repetition of petition language. If an expert asserts an element was 'well-known,' identify one or more prior art references in the declaration that corroborate that assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental information submitted within one month of institution (37 C.F.R. § 42.123(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may file a motion to submit supplemental information if the request for authorization is made within one month of the date the trial is instituted and the supplemental information is relevant to a claim for which trial has been instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond the regulatory threshold, practitioners should argue that the supplemental information does not change the asserted invalidity grounds or that the petitioner reasonably could not have submitted the information with the petition. Request authorization within 30 days and explain relevance (for example, an expert declaration clarifying a claim term).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental information submitted more than one month after institution (37 C.F.R. § 42.123(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: For supplemental information filed more than one month after institution, the party must request authorization and the motion must show why the supplemental information reasonably could not have been obtained earlier and that consideration of it would be in the interests of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address both 'foreseeability' (why it could not have been obtained earlier, e.g., evidence arising from reply declarations or deposition) and 'interests of justice' factors (see separate rubric entries). Expect a higher burden for late submissions and supply strong factual explanations and diligence evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreseeability standard for late supplemental information
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels may focus on whether the need for the evidence was foreseeable and whether the submitting party reasonably could have obtained it earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If new exhibits or evidence arise in reply declarations or during depositions that could not reasonably have been obtained earlier, emphasize that the argument/evidence was unforeseeable and that admission serves the interests of justice (e.g., allows Board to weigh credibility and completes the record). Cite examples such as Group III Int’l v. Targus Int’l.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interests of justice factors for supplemental information
rubrics_metrics.description: When weighing the interests of justice, the Board may consider: whether the supplemental information did not change the authorized grounds or add grounds; whether it was merely additional evidence related to a relevant exhibit; whether it was not withheld intentionally; whether the submitting party made continuous attempts to obtain it; whether submission would not limit the Board’s ability to complete proceedings timely; and whether the opposing party will suffer undue prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address these factors in a motion to supplement: demonstrate diligence, minimal prejudice, lack of intentional withholding, and that the evidence will aid the Board without disrupting the schedule. Case citations include Biomarin Pharm. v. Genzyme and Shire Development v. Lucerne Biosciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental information not relevant to an instituted claim (37 C.F.R. § 42.123(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party seeking to submit supplemental information not relevant to a claim for which the Board has instituted trial must request authorization and show why the information could not have been obtained earlier and that consideration would be in the interests of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such submissions may be used to resolve issues like real-party-in-interest or privity that linger after institution; explain why the evidence is necessary and meets the interests-of-justice factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental information that modifies originally presented grounds may be denied
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may deny requests to submit supplemental information if it effectively modifies the originally presented grounds, even if the request otherwise meets the regulatory requirements under § 42.123(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may not use supplemental information to 'bolster' the petition by adding new analysis or omitted claims; supplemental filings cannot be a vehicle to correct fundamental errors or omissions in the original petition (see Nanobebe US Inc. v. Mayborn (UK) Ltd.). Explain why the submission does not add new grounds or analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited scope of discovery in IPR (35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(5) and 37 C.F.R. § 42.51)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery in IPR proceedings is limited to depositions of declarants and what is otherwise necessary in the interest of justice. Parties may agree to additional discovery or move for it on a showing that it is in the interests of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect narrow, expedited discovery by default; requests for broader discovery must be justified under the Garmin factors and, where possible, agreed to by the parties. Typical additional discovery arises in less-common fact patterns (RPI/privity, objective indicia of non-obviousness, indemnification agreements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Garmin factors for additional discovery (Garmin Int’l v. Cuozzo)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether admission of evidence is in the interest of justice, the Board considers whether: (1) there is more than a possibility that something useful will be discovered; (2) the requests do not seek the other party’s litigation positions and underlying basis; (3) the requesting party can generate equivalent information by other means; (4) the requests include easily understandable instructions; and (5) the requests are not overly burdensome to answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame discovery requests to satisfy each Garmin factor: show a specific basis that useful information likely exists, avoid requests that would elicit litigation strategy, explain why the information cannot be obtained by other means, write clear instructions, and tailor requests to avoid undue burden. Cite the five-factor list from IPR2012-00001.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowly tailored discovery requests and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery requests should be specific and not 'cast too wide of a net'; explain what is sought, why it is sought, how it relates to the case, and why equivalent information is not available by other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Netlist v. Samsung example shows narrowly tailored requests are granted while broad, vague requests are denied. Avoid asking for 'any' agreements or speculative fishing expeditions; tie requests to particular products, timeframes, or issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft expert declarations and protection from discovery (work product / privilege)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft declarations generally expose attorneys’ mental processes and are protected work product until filed; FRCP 26 allows discovery of 'facts and data' but not mental impressions or expert opinion evidence based on facts and data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If opposing counsel seeks drafts, assert work product/protection unless there is a clear waiver beyond inadvertent, limited disclosure. Limit waiver arguments to the limited portions actually disclosed; avoid broad waiver by careful deposition practice and document handling. Cite Twitter, Inc. v. PARC and IPR2021-01398.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness requirement for discovery requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties seeking additional discovery should submit requests promptly after the need is identified; delay in seeking relief may justify denial, and requests cannot be used to remedy defects in earlier filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not wait until late stages to request discovery that could have been sought earlier. Demonstrate why the need arose at the time requested, avoid 'sandbagging,' and consider the expedited nature of IPR and the Board’s scheduling constraints (see Walmart v. Power Concepts and Belden v. Berk-Tek).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite pre-motion objections for motions to exclude (37 C.F.R. § 42.64)
rubrics_metrics.description: To bring a motion to exclude, the moving party must have timely served objections to the relevant evidence during the proceedings: object during a deposition for deposition evidence; file objections to other evidence during preliminary proceeding within ten business days of institution; once trial is instituted, file objections within five business days of service of the evidence. An objection must identify the grounds with 'sufficient particularity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serve objections timely and with sufficient detail to allow cure by supplemental evidence. The adverse party may supply supplemental evidence within ten business days to address the objection. Follow the procedural timelines and particularity requirements in § 42.64.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on motions to exclude
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to exclude may not be used to challenge the sufficiency of the proffered evidence or the weight that should be given to the evidence; motions to exclude should challenge admissibility grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use motions to exclude to press admissibility defects (authentication, hearsay, unavailability), not to second-guess the probative weight. Consider the low overall success rate of motions to exclude and prioritize objections to evidence that are truly critical to admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to exclude: typical successful bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Some issues on which motions to exclude have been successful include lack of authenticity of an identified document, inadmissible hearsay, and declarations whose authors are unavailable for deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a piece of evidence goes 'to the heart' of a dispute (e.g., whether a reference is prior art) and is unauthenticated or hearsay, a motion to exclude has a higher chance of success. Examples include TRW Automotive (authentication), Asetek Danmark (hearsay), and Vudu v. Ideahub (unavailable declarant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert-qualification based motions to exclude
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Kyocera, an expert who is not qualified as a POSITA may be excluded; Kyocera does not require an expert to have the relevant experience as of the critical date in all circumstances, but a lack of POSITA qualifications can be grounds for exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether experts meet proposed POSITA definitions under competing definitions; consider attacking qualifications if there is a plausible basis. Note that many panels have refused to exclude experts who acquired relevant skills after the critical date, so tailor qualification challenges accordingly and cite post-Kyocera case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic reasons to file motions to exclude despite low success rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions to exclude are often denied (about a 90+% denial rate), but filing them may influence the panel to accord little or no weight to the evidence and preserves the issue for appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the low success rate against potential strategic benefits: pressuring the panel, diminishing the evidentiary weight even if the motion is denied, and preserving appellate issues. Prioritize motions where admissibility defects are clear and central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to strike: appropriate grounds and authorization timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions to strike may be used to strike portions of an opposing party’s briefing that raise new issues, are accompanied by belatedly presented evidence, or exceed the proper scope of a reply/sur-reply. A party should request Board authorization to file the motion quickly, generally within one week of the allegedly improper submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initiate a meet-and-confer promptly, request authorization quickly (failure to do so may lead to denial of authorization), and ensure the requested relief is specific and limited. Wholesale striking of briefs is exceptional and unlikely; tailor strikes to discrete portions. See PTAB Consolidated Trial Practice Guide 2019.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success considerations and strategy for motions to strike
rubrics_metrics.description: The success rate of motions to strike depends on the obviousness of the violation; strikes are more likely when new evidence is submitted with a sur-reply, and less likely when premised on papers exceeding proper scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the violation is clear and whether the record already rebuts the new material or whether opportunity remains to respond (e.g., via reply or observations). If the violation is not clear-cut, consider alternative relief (additional briefing, request for observations) to avoid spotlighting a vulnerability. Examples: Satco Prods. (struck new evidence with sur-reply) vs. Amphenol (denied).
